chunks: "A system on module is a small board that packages a SoC together with the parts that are hardest to design around it: the DRAM, boot flash, the power-management chip, and often wireless.
It plugs into your own carrier board through a connector or castellated edges. So the SoC is the silicon, and the SoM is a ready-made mini computer built around that silicon.
The advantages are speed and risk.

The module vendor has already done the high-speed DDR layout, the power sequencing, the signal-integrity validation and the Linux or Android board-support package, so you design just the carrier, which is often a simple four-layer board with your connectors and sensors.
It can reduce time to market by months, and some modules are pre-certified for wireless regulations.
The cost is that you pay for that integration on every unit, and you're locked into the module's form factor, pinout and vendor.
At high volume, the per-unit premium adds up and a chip-down design with the same SoC will be cheaper, smaller, and optimized for your product.
So I'd use a SoM for low to medium volume, tight schedules or when the team lacks high-speed layout experience, and do chip-down once volume justifies the extra NRE.
A break-even calculation tells you where that is."
